items.title: NYT has responded to my post by claiming that I’m “spreading conspiracy theories.” But which of us is the one traffickin
items.content:
NYT has responded to my post by claiming that I’m “spreading conspiracy theories.” But which of us is the one trafficking in unsubstantiated allegations? 

Recent coverage (including CNN, which I QT’d) shows:

— The intelligence community has not established conclusive evidence that Alice Huang knowingly acted as a spy or funneled information to Beijing.

— There is internal disagreement about the strength of the evidence and whether she was recruited by the MSS.

— Attorney General Todd Blanche has said on the record that the Justice Department, he, and FBI Director Patel have reached no conclusions about “who she is or is not.”

— Some officials at ODNI and CIA have indicated the “Chinese spy” label is not fully accurate or is “over-torqued” based on the available intercepts and collection.

— Incoming House Intelligence Chairman Jim Himes, a Democrat, said it was still unclear whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy immediately after he was briefed. 

NYT’s stories (which have alleged “Chinese spy” dozens of times) have relied exclusively on anonymous officials. No official has gone on the record affirming it as established fact, and the more recent reporting reflects greater caution and disagreement inside the government. 

So when I point out that the spy narrative is unconfirmed and increasingly contested, that is not a conspiracy theory. It’s a growing body of evidence that indicts the NYT’s reporting.

Developing a drug takes years, and most candidates never reach patients.

Amortizing the cost of failed drugs across stages, the present value cost of developing a drug is close to $2B. The process takes 13 years on average, with rising clinical trial costs putting further pressure on R&D productivity.

AI could improve those economics by increasing the probability of success and reducing development time, from identifying promising molecules to designing clinical trials and improving patient recruitment.

That may enable companies to pursue therapeutic targets and indications that might otherwise have been uneconomical.

items.content:
to be or not to be like Jensen Huang?

1963
- he was born in Tainan

1973
- his parents sent him to the US at 9 with his older brother to live with their uncle.
- his uncle thought he had found them a good boarding school, but it was a reform school in Kentucky.
- his daily job there was cleaning the toilets.
- his roommate was 17 and had knife scars from fights.
- Jensen taught him to read, and in return he taught Jensen to bench press.
- he also picked up table tennis there and got good enough to be nationally ranked as a teenager.

late 1970s
- his family reunited in Oregon.
- he worked at Denny's as a dishwasher and busboy while he was in high school.
- he skipped two grades and finished high school at 16.

1984
- he graduated in electrical engineering from Oregon State.
- his lab partner there was Lori, and he later married her.
- he went on to design chips at AMD and then at LSI Logic.

1992
- he finished a master's at Stanford while working full time.
- he started meeting two engineers, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, at a Denny's in San Jose to plan a company.

1993
- he turned 30 and they started NVIDIA.

1995
- their first chip, the NV1, flopped.

1996
- the chip they were building for Sega's next console didn't work either.
- he told Sega they couldn't deliver, and asked them to invest anyway.
- Sega put in $5M, which he later said was all the money they had.
- he laid off more than half the company, going from about 100 people to 40.
- for years after that, he opened meetings with "our company is 30 days from going out of business".

1997
- their next chip, the RIVA 128, sold 1 million units in its first 4 months.

1999
- NVIDIA went public at $12 a share.
- they launched the GeForce 256 and called it the world's first GPU.

2000
- Microsoft picked NVIDIA to make the graphics chip for the first Xbox.

2006
- they launched CUDA so their chips could do more than games.

2008
- the market didn't understand CUDA, and NVIDIA fell below $5 billion during the financial crisis.

2012
- AlexNet, the model that kicked off modern AI, was trained on 2 NVIDIA gaming cards.

2016
- he hand-delivered his first AI supercomputer to a small nonprofit called OpenAI.

2019
- he bought the networking company Mellanox for $6.9B.

2020
- he agreed to buy Arm for $40B, and regulators killed the deal in 2022.

2022
- the stock dropped about 50% that year.
- ChatGPT launched in November, trained on NVIDIA chips.

2023
- NVIDIA hit $1 trillion.
- when someone asked if he'd start NVIDIA again, he said "I wouldn't do it".

2024
- NVIDIA passed $3 trillion and briefly became the most valuable company in the world.

2025
- in July it became the first company ever to hit $4 trillion.
- in October it became the first to hit $5 trillion.

October 2026
- the NYT reported that he was close to a woman US officials suspect is a Chinese spy.
- NVIDIA said his dealings with her were "not unusual or unexpected".

November 2026
- 3 House committee chairs asked him to explain his ties to her in a closed-door briefing.
- 3 days later he admitted he had been unfaithful to his wife.
- the board opened an investigation.
- the NYT then reported a second alleged affair, with an NVIDIA executive who reports to him.
- the WSJ reported that the board was getting ready to push him out.
- the stock kept falling.
- on November 12 he resigned as CEO, 33 years after he started NVIDIA.
- within hours, NVIDIA lost as much as $600 billion in value, before closing the day down 4.3%.
- the same day, Reuters reported a third alleged affair, with another NVIDIA employee.

so, to be or not to be like Jensen Huang?

items.title: I read the official Fable 5.2 prompting guide by Anthropic (so you don’t have to). Here’s what to delete, what to replac
items.content:
I read the official Fable 5.2 prompting guide by Anthropic (so you don’t have to). Here’s what to delete, what to replace & the prompt to copy:

✦ Delete the wrong rules you give to Claude.

1. Go to Claude instructions & memory.
2. Hunt for these 2 words: “always” & “never”.
3. Replace those words with “ask me first”.

Old: “Never change my prices.”
New: “Ask me before you delete anything.”

Finish the whole job before you stop. Don't offer to continue: continue.

Ask me before you delete anything.

Fable obeys “never” to the letter, even after you say yes. And “keep every sentence under 15 words” can make its writing AI. No one writes like this anyway.

✦ Say exactly what Claude should change.

1. State the goal.
2. Give it the files & context it needs.
3. Say what it can change.

Old: “Go.”
New: “Yes, rewrite the 3 welcome emails. Leave the invoice template alone.”

“Go” isn’t enough. Fable applies your words as written.

✦ Tell Claude to finish the entire job.

Add this to the prompt:

“Finish the whole job before you stop. Don't offer to continue: continue. Ask me before you delete anything.”

Then, ask for a report you can read:

“End with a recap for someone who saw none of the work: key points first, plain words.”

And lastely, check what changed before you use it.

✦ Now put it together:

Step 1. Open my guide:
https://t.co/i6lq7fjpS1
Step 2. Copy the planning prompt. Fill in your goal, context and limits.
Step 3. Let Fable plan the project. Don’t ask it to build yet.
Step 4. Still on Fable, paste the handoff prompt from the guide.
Step 5. Open a NEW chat on Opus 5.5. Attach the brief. Say: “Take it from there.”

PS: Don’t switch models inside the same chat. Opus can’t read Fable’s thinking.

BAD PROMPT: “Fix my email. Don't change anything else. Go.”

BETTER PROMPT: the task + what you approve + what needs your permission.

The planning prompt and handoff prompt are both here: https://t.co/i6lq7fjpS1

Copy them before you spend your Fable limit figuring this out yourself.

If you want to become dangerously good at Claude. You have to know which Claude tool to use, when (a few features were released yesterday):

1. Full guide + prompts at: https://t.co/psB7XxAv8w.
2. Don't pay anything. It's free in the email.
3. Send it to your team's Slack or group chat.

---

1. ASK → Chat
☑ Cowork has merged in Chat.
☑ For a quick question. Add “No web search & files”

2. THINK → Opus 5.5
☑ It won't burn that many tokens. Use it for all chat.
☑ Make it as your default model.

3. SPEED → Low effort
☑ For grammar, reformatting & translations.
☑ Lower effort for faster speed, never the model.

4. REASON → High effort
☑ For one-shot, super-ambitious work.
☑ Make it your default. Never Extra. Never Max.

5. DELEGATE → Auto mode
☑ Switch Manual to Auto. Your life will be better.
☑ Claude without your permission every second.

6. SHIP → Claude Code
☑ The Code tab in the Claude desktop app.
☑ Sites with GitHub + Vercel. Never coming back

7. FINISH → /goal command
☑ Tell Claude what “done” means.
☑ “/goal [task] until [result], or stop after 100 turns.”

8. SLIDES → Claude Design > Slides
☑ Claude Left bar > Design > Slides.
☑ Plan the outline in text first. Then: “Build this exact deck.” You can even give your brandkit.

9. MOCKUP → Claude Design
☑ Upload references. Prompt until you like it.
☑ Send a screenshot instead of describing.

10. ANIMATE → Claude Motion
☑ Type /motion in the chat.
☑ Say who watches, where & how long.
☑ Export to MP4.

11. ANALYZE → Claude Dashboards
☑ Attach a CSV or connect your data warehouse.
☑ Ask a question, not for a chart. Click any number.

12. RENDER → HTML Artifacts
☑ Prompt “Make it an HTML page.”
☑ Opens on your phone. Shared as a link.

13. BROWSE → Claude in Chrome
☑ Browsing agent to read any page.
☑ It can click on things, instead of just talking.

14. CLICK → Computer Use
☑ It clicks, types & works in your desktop apps.
☑ For native apps. Websites go through Chrome.

15. WRITE → Claude Docs (new)
☑ Claude Artifacts → Claude Docs.
☑ Use Claude Sheets, Data, and whiteboards.

15. SEARCH → Web Search
☑ Claude can decide when to search by itself.
☑ It reads the live web before answering.

16. INVESTIGATE → Research
☑ Type /deep-research or toggle it on the ‘+’.
☑ Don't use for one source, only when you need 20+ sources.

17. TRIGGER → Skills
☑ Go to Customize → Skills. Delete the old ones.
☑ Those skills are likely built for older models and can make answers worse.

18. STACK → Plugins
☑ Customize → Plugins. Bundles for legal, sales, finance.
☑ Try commercial-legal: NDAs rated green, yellow or red.

19. PERSIST → Projects
☑ One Project per client. Turn off account memory inside.
☑ Files in Projects are cached, so they count less.

20. REMEMBER → Memory
☑ Keep it on: 28% better in Anthropic’s own test.
☑ Keep it short. Clean it to under 30 lines.

21. REWIND → Edit your prompt
☑ A bad answer poisons the chat. Claude rereads it every turn.
☑ Don’t argue. Click Edit on your message, then Save.

Five non-coding methods I use to make my AI adversarial reviews more helpful:

1/ Multiple personas as subagents
I have
items.content:
Five non-coding methods I use to make my AI adversarial reviews more helpful:

1/ Multiple personas as subagents
I have Claude spin up three separate subagents, each one a different reviewer: someone who loves our product and uses it for everything, someone who hates our product and wants to destroy us, and someone who has no idea what’s going on and keeps making mistakes. In product reviews, you can combine this with your customer avatar reviews (ie descriptions of your 5 ideal buyers).

2/ Make the reviews multimodal
Ask AI to not only review the PRD or product as these personas, but also to record actual video walkthroughs as the persona, take screenshots, tweet fake tweets about it. It's not enough to just review in text format. Also ask them to review it multiple times. 

3/ Use all your subscriptions
Ask other AI systems to review it with those personas or to invent personas and do the same combo of steps one and two or just to review it for issues/bugs/errors. If you built it in Claude, have Codex review. If you built in Codex, have Antigravity review, etc.

4/ Multilayered judging
The main agent collects all the feedback from the personas and reviews the work itself. Pretty much everyone stops there. Gremlin mode: make the main agent pass it BACK to the subagents to review again, who then pass it BACK to the main agent to collate. Not enough people are playing AI as a judge or AI ping-pong as my team calls it. You can still ask for the full and complete list of feedback points and mark out which ones were added/removed at each switch. 

5/ Tell the AI it’s someone else’s work
This one is more anecdotal, but I find the review meaningfully improves when the AI thinks the work isn’t mine. So instead of “review this email draft,” try “review this email draft - it’s written by my cousin who always says the wrong thing.” Or instead of “review this app and make it better,” try “hey review this app - my best friend made it and more than anything, even if it means disappointing her in the short-term, I want her to succeed.”

Years ago, when Anthropic first rolled out Claude, they told the world they wanted Claude to be the three Hs: helpful, honest, and harmless. I believe OpenAI had essentially the same three, just with synonyms.

My theory for the fifth tip above centers on “helpful.” When it’s my work, helpful immediately translates to compliment me. Model sycophancy is poison for outcomes imo, though it has certainly gotten better over time.

Take your name off your work (temporarily).

Then loop it again.

items.content:
Don't use Claude until you read this: 

(then send it to your entire team)

> first, switch this on (nothing works without it)
> settings → capabilities → "Create and edit files"
> on Enterprise? your admin has to turn each tool
> Go to organization settings → then artifacts
> on Free plan: you still get Docs, Slides & Design
> everything you make gets stored in the Artifacts tab (left sidebar)

CLAUDE MOTION (the animated video one)

> never let Claude invent your facts. Instead
> attach the report, your logo, your screenshots
> add this line to every prompt:
"One idea per scene. Max 8 words on screen."
> if it's for Reels? ask for vertical, 1080 × 1920
> the music is muted by default. click the speaker
> To have it more polished. open it in Adobe, Descript or Runway

CLAUDE DATA (it was called Dashboards)

> it needs a live connection to your data
> if you want only a CSV, use Claude Sheets instead
> start with this prompt:

"I need to decide [the decision]. Put the 3 numbers that matter most at the top, each compared with last month. Then show me why: break them down by [channel / team / region]. Tell me every assumption you made."

> then change it by asking: "Add a filter for region."
> your data team can certify a query
> the chart then gets a "certified" badge

CLAUDE SHEETS

> every cell gets outlined, in case Claude corrects it
> for wrong edit? click on version history to restore
> limit: 100,000 cells per sheet. no pivot tables
> read-only on your phone
> a sheet can't feed a dashboard (yet)

CLAUDE WHITEBOARDS 

> drag a box around one area > ask about that part
> Claude only reads what's on the board, not apps
> so paste your context on the board first
> "follow" a teammate to see what they see
> when done, send it to Miro or export a PNG

CLAUDE MEETINGS

> owner: organization settings → products → Claude Meetings
> auto-join: settings → capabilities → Meetings
> pick "all meetings" or "all except one-on-ones"
> to not interrupt, type your ask in the Meet chat
> it keeps the transcript, not the audio
> notes & transcripts are free during the beta
> a week later, ask in any chat: "what did we decide about pricing?"

BONUS: chain them

> on a whiteboard: "turn this board into a deck"
> in Data: ask for a short narrated video of your dashboard
> and Claude Design closes on December 14
> move your projects into the Artifacts tab before that

I could tell you how hard Claude is. Very hard.
I could tell you that you are behind. Very behind.
I could tell you that Claude is full of secrets & mysteries. Only I have the answers.

But I don't.

I respect your time. You are a busy professional.

AI is getting easier with time. Not harder.

You just need to know how to start properly. Like a bike with wheels.

And if you don't know where to start, I have good news for you. I am fixing these two in my free newsletter: https://t.co/psB7XxAv8w.

Nvidia should have died in 1997. A $1 million fake chip saved it.

The man who bought it resigned from Nvidia this week.
items.content:
Nvidia should have died in 1997. A $1 million fake chip saved it.

The man who bought it resigned from Nvidia this week. His name is Jensen Huang.

In 1996, Nvidia was dying. Its first chip, the NV1, flopped. A second chip for Sega was abandoned. Jensen cut the company from about 100 people to around 40.

He had one more shot. It was called the RIVA 128.

Normally you design a chip, pay to build a physical prototype, test it, fix it, and build another. That takes months. He didn't have months.

So he bought a hardware emulator from a struggling company called IKOS for about $1 million. A fake chip built in code, the size of a refrigerator.

It was so slow the team sat waiting for a single frame of Windows to draw. They moved the ping-pong table so it would fit in the break room.

> They ran every game and driver they had on it
> They caught the bugs before any real chip existed
> Then Jensen skipped the prototype and went straight to mass production
> No one in the industry had done that before

If the first chips came back broken, Nvidia was finished.

They worked.

The RIVA 128 shipped in August 1997 with about one month of payroll left. It sold about a million units in four months. Nvidia went public in 1999.

For years, Jensen opened internal presentations with the same line: "Our company is thirty days from going out of business."

On November 12, 2026, Nvidia announced his resignation. He left a company worth about $4 trillion.

Most people wait for a perfect prototype before they ship anything. The company that powers AI exists because one founder couldn't afford to.

Would you have bet the company on the fake chip? Yes or no.

items.content:
i genuinely cannot stand people who keep saying they can't make money and then come up with the most bullshit excuses ever like "i don't have enough capital", "i have school", "i don't have time" or "it's all a scam"

and what pisses me off the most is when i hear this from people living in the US. bro you're literally living in one of the best places in the world for opportunities. i got rejected from 4 SIX FIGURE job offers just because i don't live in the US and then i see some mf in america complaining that there's no way to make money. like brother GO FUCKING TRY. try SaaS, mobile apps, sales, design, literally anything. if making money was easy everyone would be rich but that's not how life works

and i'm not saying this as someone who grew up rich or had everything handed to him. i literally grew up in a third world country. my family was so poor at one point that 3 of us were sleeping on ONE mattress and sometimes we didn't even have enough money for food. yk how that feels as a kid? seeing your family struggling and knowing you can't do shit about it? but instead of sitting there crying about how unfair life was i started trying everything i could

when AI started taking off i was selling homework to kids at school for 50 cents and the funniest part is that i was literally an F grade student myself. but that stupid little business taught me how to sell and talk to people, which turned out to be one of the most valuable skills i've ever learned

then i joined @blakeandersonw's discord community and started meeting some of the most amazing people i've ever known. i kept talking to people, making connections and trying to be useful until eventually @porterstanleyai trusted me to build a SaaS for him

and here's the crazy part. I DIDN'T EVEN KNOW HOW TO FUCKING CODE. i couldn't even write basic HTML at the time. so i spent an entire week learning how to code from basically zero, making a shit ton of mistakes and trying to figure everything out. i was literally competing with people who had CS degrees from HARVARD and somehow i was the one who got the role

after that i kept learning actual development, got certifications from Google and IBM and became way better at what i was doing. he paid me my first $1k and eventually vouched for me to other people which helped me make my first $3k. ALL OF THIS AT 14 BTW. and that was the moment i realized making real money online was actually possible

but it wasn't all good after that. for basically the next year i barely made $200 because i kept fucking things up. my communication was terrible, i lost opportunities and had to relearn a lot of things. but i didn't stop trying

then january 2026 came and i genuinely had no fucking idea what to build or how to start making money again. so instead of spending months thinking about the perfect business idea i literally opened Claude, talked to it for like 20 minutes and gave it a big ass prompt asking it to come up with a good mobile app idea that i could actually build

it gave me an idea for a mental wellness app which i called Mira AI. i didn't do some crazy market research or spend thousands building it. i literally told Claude to create a simple waitlist website and in LESS THAN AN HOUR i had a pretty good looking website ready to go

then i went on Reddit and made a simple post talking about a problem i personally had and how i wished there was an app that could help with it. i didn't even promote anything at first, i just explained the problem and asked if other people felt the same way

and guess what? a shit ton of people started commenting that they had the exact same problem and wished something like this existed. the post ended up getting around 100K VIEWS

so i went back, edited the post and added my website link. and btw the website was literally hosted on a free subdomain, i didn't even spend money buying a domain

then i got a friend to help me set up Stripe, created a $50 preorder link and started messaging people who had joined my waitlist. FOUR PEOPLE ACTUALLY PAID ME $50 EACH FOR AN APP THAT WASN'T EVEN BUILT YET

bro imagine how crazy that felt. i went from having absolutely no idea what to build to having people willing to pay for something i came up with while talking to Claude for 20 minutes

and the entire thing started with basically ZERO CAPITAL

i took that money and started putting it back into myself. trying new things, fixing my mistakes, meeting more people and finding other clients. i wasn't trying to make some perfect million dollar startup, i was just trying to figure out how to make my next dollar

and eventually things started working out. in january 2026 i made around $1k, february i did around $3k in total revenue, then $5k, then $7k until eventually i reached around $10k a month

and i was doing all of this while managing school, working on other businesses, dealing with family responsibilities, playing 2 sports and going to the gym. i eventually had to cut off a lot of things and focus on what actually mattered because trying to do everything at once was making everything harder

and when i finally hit $10k i genuinely thought i'd made it. i thought i could literally retire off that money

then i started looking at where all my money had gone and realized basically everything i worked for was GONE. $2k for my school and my sister's school, $2k i got scammed out of, $1k lost trading, $3k in expenses over 5 months and another $2k helping my family

and just like that $10k was gone. i was making all this money but barely keeping any of it. and that's when i realized that making $10k in revenue and actually having $10k in your bank account are two completely different things

i think i have around $1k to my name rn and the funny thing is i'm not even that upset about it anymore. obviously losing money fucking sucks but the way i look at it now is completely different from how i used to

i started thinking about life like a video game. you figure out how to make your first $1k, you make mistakes, you lose money, you learn and then figure out how to make $10k. then you do the same thing trying to reach $100k. every time you fuck up you learn something that makes the next attempt easier

and that's probably the biggest thing i've learned from all of this. the money can disappear but the skills and connections you've built don't just disappear with it. i might not have much money sitting in my account rn but i know how to make money again because i've already done it before

if i had to start over again with absolutely nothing, i'd do almost the exact same thing. i'd join discord communities full of founders and people actually building shit, start talking to them, learn a valuable skill like development, design or sales and become genuinely good at it

not just pretend i'm good, ACTUALLY become someone people can trust to get shit done. because once you start building trust and making real connections you'll find opportunities you never even knew existed. that's literally how everything started for me. one discord community led to meeting someone who gave me a chance, that chance led to my first $1k, then my first $3k and eventually opportunities i couldn't have imagined before

and even with Mira AI, i didn't have some genius idea or an amazing business plan. i literally talked to an AI for 20 minutes, built a free website and made a Reddit post. that's it. obviously not every idea will work out like that but how the fuck are you supposed to know if you never even try?

and bro i'm not saying it's easy. i know how fucking hard it is when you have no money, no connections and no idea what you're doing. i've been there. i know what it feels like to see other people succeeding while you're struggling to make even $100

but you have to start somewhere. stop spending months looking for the perfect idea or waiting until you have enough capital. you don't need to build the next billion dollar company tomorrow. you just need to figure out how to make your first $100, then your first $1k, then figure out how to do it again

your first $1k might be the hardest money you'll ever make but once you understand HOW you made it, reaching $10k starts looking way more possible. not because it suddenly becomes easy but because you've already proven to yourself that you can actually do something people are willing to pay for

and please stop thinking everyone making money online had some secret advantage. some people definitely do, but a lot of people just tried more things than you did, failed more times than you did and kept going when nothing was working

items.content:
build a walkable oil-painting world with claude Fable 5.2 + Three.js...

the trick is painting the world with brush strokes, not filtering a finished frame

here’s the workflow:

- step 1: fable 5.2: prompt it to set up a three.js 0.186 + webgl2 scene with a third-person camera
- step 2: rapier: add physics for walking, sprinting and jumping on the terrain
- step 3: makehuman: drop in the base character from the patch starter kit
- step 4: quaternius animation library + patch clips: add idle, walk, run and jump
- step 5: fable 5.2 + custom glsl shaders: turn every object into brush strokes with 3 paint colors
- step 6: glsl shaders: add lighting, fog, falling snow and the glowing aurora
- step 7: fable 5.2: build the snowy ridge, spruces and cabin out of strokes
- step 8: https://t.co/KD9HzU5pgx: publish the playable demo and the open-source code

who does what:

> Fable 5.2: writes the scene and the shaders
> Three.js: renders it in the browser
> GLSL shaders: the oil-paint look
> Rapier: physics
> MakeHuman + Quaternius: the character and its animations
> Patch gg: publishing

stroke order can never depend on the camera. if it does, the paint crawls every time you move
